vignette:
Narin is an 18-year-old Cambodian American photographer who came to treatment looking older than his age, wiry and keyed up, scanning the hallway each time a door shut. He had been in combat only months earlier, attached in a support role that left him carrying a camera as often as supplies, documenting damage and movement in a setting where the line between observer and target vanished quickly. The moment that returns most often began in a village street after a burst of gunfire. He remembers crouching behind a broken wall with two other young men from his unit while civilians ran past them. One of the men beside him was hit. Narin can still see the red dust jumping from the wall, hear the concussive crack, and feel the camera strap biting into his neck as he lunged forward and then froze. What has fixed itself in him is the conviction that he should have moved faster, dragged the others out, done something decisive. Instead, he remembers being caught between photographing what was happening and trying to survive it, and he has come to regard that hesitation as a moral failure rather than the paralysis of terror.

In the weeks after he returned to the U.S., that conclusion hardened into a broader way of seeing himself and everyone around him. He had come to believe he had failed to protect people and that this said something permanent about him: that he did not belong with other teenagers, not with civilians, not even with family who spoke to him as if he were simply home from a trip. The same belief spread outward into mistrust. If he had been wrong about who was safe there, he felt he could be wrong anywhere, and he stopped assuming anyone meant well. From that stance, his body stayed primed. He could not relax even in his bedroom. A car backfiring outside his apartment or a metal tray dropped in a café made him jump violently, shoulders up, heart racing before he knew why. He has also begun taking risks that alarm his family-speeding on his motorcycle, walking alone late at night in rough parts of the city-because some part of him feels that vigilance and danger fit him better than ordinary safety, and because he no longer trusts safety when it is offered.

Those same appraisals shape the way the memories come. When Narin thinks, even briefly, "I failed them," the scene returns with a force that feels more real than normal remembering, as if the street has replaced the present. He does not describe it as recalling the event so much as being dropped back into it. What comes with the image is not only fear but rage-at himself for freezing, at the chain of command, at the men who fired, at bystanders who kept running. He can be editing photos at work and catch the smell of overheated electronics from his studio lights, and suddenly the hot dust and burned air of that day are there in full detail without warning. Because he already expects betrayal and feels cut off from everyone around him, these intrusions land in a mind prepared to read them as proof: proof that he is the one who failed, proof that nowhere is truly safe, proof that no one around him can understand what he carries.

The memories in turn deepen those beliefs. Each time he is transported back into that street, what frightens him most is not only the vividness but how certain he feels in those moments that the event reveals his true character. After an episode he is more convinced that he cannot trust people and less able to imagine belonging anywhere outside that violent world. He has stopped meeting friends unless absolutely necessary. When his mother asks where he is going, he hears intrusion rather than concern. He keeps his camera work solitary now, preferring night shoots and abandoned industrial spaces, places where he can watch every entrance.

That constant state of alarm also makes the memories more likely. At assignments, ordinary sounds-a shutter clack, a delivery truck banging its gate-make him flinch and whip around. Once he is already on edge, scanning for danger, almost anything in the environment can ignite the whole scene from combat. The instant replay leaves him furious and raw, and afterward he is harsher with himself, more certain he failed and that other people are naïve or untrustworthy for acting as if the world is benign. The loop has tightened enough that his work has started to suffer; clients have complained that he abruptly leaves shoots, and he recently scared an assistant by shoving past him when a light stand crashed to the floor.

He finally sought help after nearly causing a serious accident while driving too fast after being startled by a loud exhaust pop that sent him straight back to the village street. What brought him in was not only fear of losing control, but the dawning sense that he is building a life organized entirely around that moment. He says he wants to know whether it is possible to remember what happened without being swallowed by it, though he is not sure he deserves that relief.
